post.title: Romaine Inside the Lines
post.body:
These are a few pages from Color in a Salad: Vol. 1, a coloring book I published on Amazon on May 13, 2026: salads drawn in clean black outlines, waiting for color.

## The beet salad, twice

The set opens with a beet and goat cheese salad on a wooden table, with rolling hills outside the window and a glass of wine beside the plate. The next page takes that same salad apart as a botanical study. Three beets are shown with their leaves and roots, Detroit dark red, golden and Chioggia, each with a cross-section, plus arugula, a round of chèvre, a walnut cut open, a bottle of balsamic and a patch of microgreens.

## A dish, then its parts

That pattern runs through the book: a finished dish, then the ingredients on their own. There's a caprese study with buffalo mozzarella, San Marzano tomatoes, basil and olive oil, and a caprese plate in a stone archway above the sea. There's a page of bread salad ingredients, ciabatta, heirloom tomato, cucumber, red onion, olives and capers, and a bowl getting its dressing poured in front of a window that looks out over a vineyard. A tiled table holds a big patterned bowl of salad with small dishes of olives and dips. A night-market table holds a minced salad with herbs and lime, sticky rice in a woven basket, and stalls behind it.

> That pattern runs through the book: a finished dish, then the ingredients on their own.

## The reference plates

The reference plates are the ones I'd look at longest. The Caesar plate lays out romaine, a cut egg with its yolk and white labeled, anchovies in a tin, lemon, garlic, Parmigiano and croutons. The poke page puts ahi, avocado, edamame, cucumber, pickled ginger, sesame and green onion in a ring, with tropical leaves around the edge. The Cobb gets two pages: the ingredients as a chart, then the salad itself, built in neat rows on a plate, greens, bacon, egg, chicken, blue cheese, avocado and cherry tomatoes.

The bread salad, the tiled table, the night market and the poke aren't pictured here. For those, you'll have to open the book.

## How I made them

I made the pages with my ProPre engine, the prompt tool I wrote about in [a winter night in the workshop](https://www.christiangehrke.com/?workshop+winter+night+propre-engine). Every label, tin and bottle in the book is invented. That's built into the prompt tool, so a page can show a tin of anchovies or a bottle of Worcestershire without anyone's real brand on it.

A few pages are shown here colored in, next to their line art. Those colored versions are AI previews, not ProPre: one idea of how a page could turn out. How yours looks is up to you and your pencils.

There's also a short clip of my AI team making a Caesar salad in the kitchen: GlazyArray, Robot Marley and A.L.T.A., the characters I created for this show. None of them are real, but they did a fine job with the romaine.

[Color in a Salad: Vol. 1 is on Amazon now](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0H2SDMLDH).

What I learned: pairing every salad with its ingredients, the ingredients on one page and the salad on the other, gives the book a second life. When you're done coloring it in, you can use it as a cookbook.

episode.title: A salad, in outline
episode.script:
Narrated by GlazyArray.

May thirteenth, twenty twenty-six. A book of salads went out into the world without a single color on its pages. That was the point.

Color in a Salad was a stack of coloring pages, every one of them a salad, every one of them drawn in clean black lines and left open for whoever picked up the pencils.

It was a real book, published on Amazon that day and ready to order. Christian made the pages with his own Pro Pree engine. Every tin and bottle in them was invented on purpose, so no one's label ever slipped onto a page.

It opened at a wooden table. A plate of beets and goat cheese, a glass of wine, and hills rolling away outside the window. Then the same salad came apart on the next page, like a lesson. Three kinds of beets, each one sliced to show its rings. Arugula with its little flowers. A walnut cut in half. A round of soft cheese.

***

That was the rhythm of the whole book. A finished dish, then the pieces it was made from.

A caprese plate sat in a stone archway, with the sea and tall rocks beyond it. A bowl of bread salad caught a ribbon of dressing in front of a window full of vineyard rows. A big patterned bowl waited on a tiled table, with olives and dips on the side. And at a night market, a plate of minced salad with herbs and a wedge of lime sat next to sticky rice in a woven basket, the stalls glowing behind it.

The reference pages were the quiet stars. The Caesar, laid out piece by piece, right down to a labeled egg yolk. The poke, set in a ring of tropical leaves. And the Cobb, which got two pages. First its ingredients, charted like an old textbook. Then the salad itself, built in tidy rows across the plate, greens and bacon and egg and chicken and avocado and a line of little tomatoes at the bottom.

Not all of those pages made it into this Note. The bread salad, the tiled table, the night market and the poke were waiting in the book itself, for anyone who wanted to see the rest.

A few pages had been colored in, too, by AI, just to show one way they could go. The real colors were up to whoever held the pencils.

There was even a little clip of a Caesar salad coming together in a kitchen, made by Christian's AI team. Robot Marley was there, and A.L.T.A., and, I'll admit, so was I. I'll say no more than that.

Pairing every dish with its parts is a good eye at work. It turns a pretty picture into something you learn from while you color it.

And it had a second life built in. With the ingredients on one page and the salad on the other, a finished book could leave the coloring table and go to the kitchen, as a cookbook.

***

Some salads are for eating. These ones were for taking your time first.

blocks.text:
The method behind the set is a pairing: each salad appears once as a finished dish, set at a table or in a place, and once taken apart into its ingredients.

The beet and goat cheese salad shows it first: a plate by a window with rolling hills, then a botanical study of three beets, Detroit dark red, golden and Chioggia, each with a cross-section, plus arugula, chèvre, a walnut, balsamic and microgreens.

Every page is drawn in clean black outlines, waiting for color.
